lessons.title: What Is a View
lessons.concept: A view is a virtual table based on the result of a SQL query. It does not store data itself (in most basic cases) but presents data from one or more underlying tables. Views can simplify complex queries, provide a consistent interface, and help with access control.
lessons.formula: CREATE VIEW view_name AS SELECT ...; Query: SELECT * FROM view_name; Drop: DROP VIEW view_name;
lessons.worked_example: CREATE VIEW active_users AS SELECT id,name FROM users WHERE status='active'; then SELECT * FROM active_users returns only active users without repeating the filter.
mistakes: Assuming a view always stores a physical copy of data
Expecting all views to be updatable in every case
Forgetting that changes in base tables are reflected in view results
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Benefits and Limitations
lessons.concept: Views simplify repeated query logic, improve readability, and can restrict exposure to specific columns/rows. However, complex views may impact performance, and not all views support INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations (especially those with joins, aggregates, or derived columns).
lessons.formula: Use cases: abstraction, security (column/row filtering), reuse. Limitation: updatability depends on view definition and DBMS rules.
lessons.worked_example: A view selecting only non-sensitive columns (id,name,department) from employees can be shared instead of the full employees table containing salary details.
mistakes: Using views as a guaranteed performance optimization without checking execution plans
Assuming every view is directly writable
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Creating and Using Views Safely
lessons.concept: Define views with clear names and explicit column lists when helpful. Understand whether the view is meant for read-only reporting or for updates. When replacing definitions, use DBMS-supported syntax (e.g., CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW where available).
lessons.formula: Readable pattern: CREATE VIEW v_name (colA,colB) AS SELECT colA,colB FROM t WHERE ...;
lessons.worked_example: If business logic changes, updating the view definition can centralize the change so dependent queries using the view remain consistent.
mistakes: Relying on SELECT * in view definitions when schema evolution can break consumers

practice.question: A SQL view is best described as:

options.A: A physical copy of a table always stored separately
options.B: A virtual table based on a query

practice.explanation: A view is a virtual table defined by a SELECT query; querying the view runs/uses that definition over underlying data (in basic cases).
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Which statement creates a view named emp_names?

options.A: CREATE VIEW emp_names AS SELECT name FROM employees;
options.C: CREATE TABLE emp_names AS VIEW employees;
options.D: SELECT VIEW emp_names AS name FROM employees;

practice.explanation: The standard syntax is CREATE VIEW view_name AS followed by a SELECT statement.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: One common benefit of views is:

options.A: They eliminate the need for base tables
options.B: They can simplify complex queries and restrict exposed columns/rows
options.C: They always make every query faster

practice.explanation: Views provide abstraction and can limit visible data, improving usability and security; performance effects depend on the case.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Are all SQL views updatable?

options.B: No, updatability depends on the view definition and DBMS rules
options.C: Yes, if they have a name
options.D: No, views can never be queried

practice.explanation: Simple views may be updatable, but views with joins, aggregates, DISTINCT, or derived columns often are not directly updatable.

practice.question: Which command removes a view?
practice.explanation: DROP VIEW is used to remove a view definition from the database.

questions.explanation: A view is defined by a query on base tables, so querying it reflects current underlying data (for standard non-materialized views).

questions.question: Which view is less likely to be directly updatable?

options.A: A view selecting a few columns from one table without aggregates
options.B: A view with GROUP BY and aggregate functions
options.C: A simple view on a single table
options.D: A view that maps columns directly

questions.explanation: Aggregations and grouping make row-to-base-row mapping ambiguous, so such views are commonly not directly updatable.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?

options.A: Views always store data and never depend on base tables
options.B: Views can encapsulate query logic for reuse
options.C: DROP VIEW deletes base table data
options.D: Views cannot be used in SELECT queries

questions.explanation: Views encapsulate SELECT logic so it can be reused easily. They do not inherently store independent data and dropping a view does not drop base tables.
